newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian govt to win by-election - poll.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian govt to win by-election - poll.

text.p: Australia's Liberal-National coalition government appears set to win in Saturday's by-election for the Sydney seat of Lindsay, according to a poll published on Friday.
The AGB McNair poll, published in The Sydney Morning Herald newspaper, found Liberal candidate Jackie Kelly has a lead of nine percent over Labor Party candidate Ross Free.
According to the poll of 1,002 voters in Lindsay, Kelly has 41 percent of first preference votes, followed by Free with 32 percent.
"The figures suggest that Labor, which forced the by-election, has gone backwards since the March 2 (federal) election," the newspaper reported.
"This is despite the government being plunged into its worst political crisis this week, with two resignations and three cabinet ministers under attack in parliament over their pecuniary interests."
The poll found that 14 percent of the voters surveyed were undecided with the remainder of the vote split between the large number of minor party candidates and independents.
The Australians Against Further Immigration candidate would receive four percent of the vote, followed by the Shooters' Party with three percent, the poll found.
"A notional distribution of those preferences has the Liberals further in front - 55 percent to 45 percent," the newspaper said.

The High Court ordered the by-election when it found that Kelly, who won the seat from Free on March 2, contravened the constitution by working for the government as an airforce member and holding dual Australia-New Zealand citizenship.
However, Liberal Party president Tony Staley said although a result such as the one suggested by the poll would be good, the party was not confident of retaining its hold on the seat.
Staley said the preference swap deal between the Labor Party and Australians Against Further Immigration meant that Kelly was likely to lose the seat.
"In short, as we distribute the preferences, that sadly means that we would narrowly lose," Staley told Australian Broadcasting Corp radio.
"A whole lot depends, therefore, on the preferences."
